name: Rice water

lead: Rice water is the milky liquid left over when rice is rinsed, soaked or boiled, used in parts of Asia as a hair rinse and skin wash, with fermented versions popular on social media. Proponents say it makes hair shinier, stronger and less prone to breakage, and that it soothes and brightens skin for a more even-looking complexion.

It carries starch plus small amounts of vitamins, minerals and amino acids. Proponents point to compounds such as inositol and ferulic acid as the reason it might smooth hair strands, reduce friction and support skin. A 2023 review of topical hair remedies popular on TikTok examined claims like these, and an encyclopedic overview describes studies of rice water itself as limited, with growth claims resting largely on accounts such as those of Yao women in China. No clinical trial of rice water for hair or skin appears in the sources reviewed.

paras: People soak or boil rice, strain off the liquid, sometimes ferment it for a day or two, then use it as a rinse after shampooing or as a face wash or toner. Users usually repeat it as part of a regular routine.

Topical use is generally treated as low risk, but no controlled safety data exist. Rice can contain arsenic, which is discussed mainly for drinking rice water, and prepared rice water can spoil if stored for long.

web.title: Rice water for hair (Medical News Today)
Can Rice Water Really Encourage Hair Growth?

chain: Starch and amino acids on skin
angle.text: Rice water is a folk beauty rinse from parts of Asia, used on hair for shine and less breakage and as a skin wash for softness and an even-looking complexion. It is popular in beauty communities, and no trials have tested it for hair or skin.

lead: Rice water is the cloudy, starchy liquid left after rice is rinsed, soaked or boiled. It carries starch along with small amounts of vitamins, minerals and amino acids leached from the grain, and it can also be left to ferment for a day or two before use.[1] It has a long history of folk use in parts of Asia as a hair rinse and skin wash, and it is also used as an oral fluid for diarrhoea.[1]

People use it for their looks in two main ways: as a hair rinse said to add shine, smoothness and strength, so that hair breaks less and appears longer and thicker, and as a skin toner said to soothe and brighten the complexion.[1][2][3] The chain proponents describe runs from coating and smoothing the hair strand, to less friction and breakage, to hair that retains length and looks fuller; one scientist quoted in Martha Stewart's coverage says it does not make hair grow faster but makes existing growth easier to see.[4]

The practice became a global beauty trend through TikTok and celebrity coverage in the early 2020s; Gulf News reported almost 87 million views for the #ricewater hashtag in 2022 and named Cardi B and Kim Kardashian among those associated with it.[3] A 2023 Cutis review of topical hair-loss remedies popular on TikTok, which included rice water alongside rosemary oil, onion juice and garlic gel, set out to examine the research behind such claims.[5]

The main published laboratory work is a 2010 study by Inamasu and colleagues on hair samples, which reported lower surface friction and higher elasticity after a rice rinse.[6] No published clinical trial has tested rice water as a cosmetic hair or skin treatment in people; related work concerns other rice-derived products.[1][2]
infobox: Hair shine and strength, skin brightening, soothing
Traditional use in China, Japan and Southeast Asia [7][6]
Red Yao women of Huangluo, China; Heian-period Japanese court women [2][3][6]

paras: Rice water is described as a milky suspension created when grains are rinsed or soaked in water, or when the starchy liquid is drained after boiling. Starch makes up most of the grain by weight, and the water also picks up minerals such as iron, zinc, magnesium and potassium and vitamins such as B2 and E in small quantities, with the profile varying by rice type and method.[1]

Three types are commonly distinguished: plain rice water from rinsing or soaking, boiled rice water drained from cooking, and fermented rice water, which is plain rice water left at room temperature for roughly 12 to 48 hours so that it turns slightly sour through microbial activity.[1] Proponents of the fermented form attribute extra benefit to the resulting acidity and probiotic content.[1] Rice water differs from rice milk, a blended beverage, and from rice bran water, which is extracted from the bran layer rather than the whole grain.[1]

Women in parts of Asia, including China, Japan and Southeast Asia, have used rice water on their hair for centuries, according to Wikipedia.[7] In Japan the practice is dated to the Heian period (794 to 1185 CE), when court women were said to keep floor-length hair healthy by bathing it in rice water.[7] Grokipedia describes use over more than a millennium in Asian cultures, including in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, and for purposes beyond cosmetics such as agriculture.[1]

The long hair of the Yao women of China, who attribute it to regular fermented rice water rinses, became the best-known modern story and helped carry the practice into global beauty media and social platforms, where fermented rice water became a recurring trend.[1][5] Rice water has also long been taken by mouth as a food for digestive illness; Wikipedia cites a 1981 Lancet letter on rice water in infantile gastroenteritis and a 1992 BMJ meta-analysis of 13 trials of rice-based oral rehydration solution, and flags the claim that it helps cholera and gastroenteritis as needing better sourcing.[7]

Accounts of the best-known traditions differ in detail. Medical News Today and Gulf News both describe the Red Yao women of Huangluo village in China, who wash with fermented rice water, though they give different average hair lengths (6 feet and 4.5 feet respectively).[2][3] Curl Centric adds that the village is listed in the Guinness World Records for the longest-haired village and that Heian-period court women used a rinse water called yu-su-ru, with surviving artwork showing floor-length hair; it presents these traditions as real but as an observation rather than a controlled comparison, because the Yao women differ from others in many ways besides their rinse.[6]

Gulf News also mentions a festive hair-washing ceremony with fermented rice water among Thai people by the Da River.[3] In the 2010s and 2020s the practice moved from regional tradition into Western and Korean-beauty discussion, hair-care blogs and then short video, where fermented rice water became a recurring trend and rice-based shampoos and serums appeared on shelves.[3][4]

sections.h: Use in hair and skin care
paras: As a hair rinse, rice water is said by proponents to reduce friction between strands, increase elasticity and help repair damaged hair, with the carbohydrate inositol often cited as the active component, so that hair breaks less and appears to retain length.[1] The best-known story in this area is the long hair of Yao women in China, who attribute it to regular fermented rice water rinses; the encyclopedic overview treats this as anecdotal rather than as measured evidence.[1]

On skin, rice water is used as a toner or wash with the stated aims of soothing irritation, brightening the complexion and supporting collagen, with ferulic acid and inositol named as relevant rice-derived components.[1] It is also listed among traditional lightening and skin-care ingredients in appearance-oriented communities.

Rice water is also used outside cosmetics, taken by mouth in some traditions for diarrhoea, and as a garden fertiliser.[1] Rice-based oral rehydration solutions have been studied in diarrhoeal disease, including cholera, and this literature concerns hydration rather than appearance.[8]

Proponents' explanations centre on inositol, a carbohydrate found in rice water that, in the 2010 Inamasu study, remained in hair after rinsing and was associated with lower surface friction and higher elasticity.[6] Martha Stewart's coverage quotes hair scientist Gaby Longsworth, who says inositol improves elasticity and reduces friction, and that the proteins in rice water are too large to penetrate the hair shaft and instead coat it.[4]

For fermented rice water, believers add that fermentation by lactic acid bacteria produces acidity and probiotic content that they say benefits hair and scalp.[1] For skin, ferulic acid and inositol are named as relevant rice-derived components, with claims of soothing, brightening and collagen support.[1]

Experts quoted in the press are divided. Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Shilpi Khetarpal has said inositol may help hair grow faster and look healthier and shinier, according to coverage of her comments, while other dermatologists and trichologists say the studies are weak or that the main effect is on the scalp.[3] Medical News Today reports that dermatologists have raised concern that heavy starches may damage hair.[2]

Descriptions of use are general and vary widely. Plain rice water is made by rinsing or soaking rice in water and keeping the cloudy liquid; boiled rice water is the liquid drained after cooking; fermented rice water is left to stand at room temperature before use.[1] People apply it as a pre-shampoo treatment, a rinse after shampoo or a scalp spray, then rinse it out, and commonly follow with conditioner.[6]

Guides such as Curl Centric and Martha Stewart's coverage describe leaving it on for roughly ten to thirty minutes and using it about weekly, with results said to take weeks of consistent use, and they advise that overuse or leaving it on overnight can leave stiff, dry hair.[4][6] Some people dilute it to lower the chance of buildup.[4][6]

No studies found that test rice water as a cosmetic hair or skin treatment in humans. The most-cited laboratory work is a 2010 study by Inamasu and colleagues in the Journal of the Society of Cosmetic Chemists of Japan, which tested rice rinse on hair samples against untreated hair and reported reduced surface friction, improved elasticity and inositol remaining in the hair after rinsing; Curl Centric notes that plain rice water left flakes on hair, so the team tested processed rice water extracts, and that all four researchers worked at a cosmetics company.[6]

A 2023 narrative review in Cutis examined the evidence behind topical hair-loss remedies circulating on social media, naming rice water among them.[5] Medical News Today reports that a 2022 systematic review of ten studies found rice bran products promising for hair growth, but that review did not examine rice water.[2] An encyclopedic overview states that research on rice water specifically is limited or concerns other rice products.[1]

Studies of related rice products exist and are not tests of rice water on hair or skin. A randomised, double-blind trial registered for fermented rice flour in atopic dermatitis involved 50 participants,[9] and a review and several trials have studied rice-based oral rehydration solutions for diarrhoea.[8]

Rice can accumulate arsenic from the soil and water in which it is grown, and the arsenic content of cooked rice has been studied in relation to cooking and washing methods.[10] Encyclopedic sources raise this as a consideration mainly for internal consumption of rice water and suggest low-arsenic rice varieties for that purpose.[1]

Because rice water is a starch-rich liquid, it can spoil. Guidance summarised in an encyclopedic overview says prepared rice water should be refrigerated for a few days at most and discarded if it develops an off smell or mold.[1] Topical safety data from controlled studies are not available.

For topical hair use, practitioners and press describe a stiffness-and-dryness effect sometimes called protein overload. Gulf News quotes dermatologist Fatima Zohra Rezgui as saying dry hair can be overloaded with protein or amino acids, causing breakage, and advising people with dry hair to use it at most monthly; she suggests normal to oily hair about weekly.[3] Curl Centric argues the effect is better described as starch and mineral buildup, since rice water's measured protein content is low, and suggests clarifying and then using half-strength rice water.[6] Gaby Longsworth says it is better suited to chemically processed or coloured hair than to fine or low-porosity hair.[4] Gulf News quotes dermatologist Wissam Addada as advising people with scalp inflammation or conditions such as psoriasis to see a specialist first.[3] Curl Centric advises skipping the fermented version on broken or inflamed skin.[6]

Rice water is a kitchen preparation rather than a regulated product, and it is made at home from rice that most households already have. Its popularity in hair-care discussion is documented by the Cutis review of TikTok hair-loss remedies, which lists it with rosemary oil, onion juice and garlic gel,[5] and by forum comments such as one on T Nation noting that people were widely using fermented rice water while that poster named minoxidil and miconazole shampoo as the only products they regarded as working.[11]

In the media the topic recurs as a hair-care trend explainer, typically featuring dermatologists or trichologists who describe the tradition, the 2010 laboratory study and the lack of trials.[2][3][4] Celebrity attention, including Cardi B and Kim Kardashian according to Gulf News, and TikTok view counts drove much of the early-2020s interest.[3]

lore.intro: Rice water is discussed mainly as a hair rinse and as a social-media hair-growth trend; on T Nation it appears as a passing mention of a current fad.[5][11]
